entries.title: What’s the Point of Running as a Republican in D.C.?
entries.summary: For this year's candidates, the reasons range from rodents to education to a need to challenge the status quo.
entries.content:
If you’re surprised to learn that a Puerto Rico-born immigration lawyer is running for local office in D.C. as a Republican, you’re probably not alone.

“I am probably one of the most unconventional Republicans you will meet,” admits Manuel Rivera.

Rivera wasn’t even a Republican until the last presidential election. Before that, he was a lifelong Democrat — a conservative one, by his own telling — who once mounted an unsuccessful bid for a seat in the Rhode Island House of Representatives.

But now he’s flying the Republican flag, and running for D.C. attorney general.

Rivera is one of seven like-minded Republican candidates vying for local office in D.C. this year, a slate that includes other similarly convention-bucking contenders. For example, a self-proclaimed Biblical Christian woman is challenging the D.C. Council chairman, who has been in office longer than she’s been alive. And a Republican will be on the ballot in Ward 1 — considered the city’s most progressive ward — for the first time in 16 years.

“This election is especially important because it represents a renewed effort by the Republican Party to offer the District’s voters a range of ideas and qualified candidates,” Rivera told The Washington Sun. “We have assembled one of the strongest Republican slates in history.”
Manuel Riviera (7792x5195, AR: 1.50)But for as strong as Rivera may think that slate is, so too are the local currents working against it. There hasn’t been a Republican elected to office in D.C. for almost two decades, and President Donald Trump’s vote share in the 2024 election barely exceeded 6%.

“It’s pointless,” said David Krucoff, who ran for the Ward 3 council seat as a moderate Republican in 2022 — notching a respectable 22% of the vote. He later became disillusioned with the party and is now an independent.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Still, turnout in the June Republican primary was higher than it has been in 14 years, a sign party leaders say is an indication of renewed local energy in the face of an inescapably tough political landscape. And many Republicans concede that even with victory unlikely, the value in running is just to offer voters something different.

“Washington, D.C. is a one-party system,” says Rivera. “I believe democracy works best when voters have a real choice. Somebody must be willing to challenge that status quo.”

Crime, Rodents and Education

The conventional wisdom in D.C. is that Rivera’s chances — like those of his fellow GOP candidates — aren’t very good in November.

Beyond the raw political reality that only 5% of the city’s 485,000 registered voters are Republicans, the party’s national brand has been on a downward trajectory in urban areas over the last three decades. There hasn’t been a Republican elected to the council since 2008.

“If you want to be a local Republican in D.C. now and generally are affiliated with the administration, that’s just not a popular thing to be,” said Krucoff.

Still, Rivera and the other GOP contenders say that D.C. voters are sophisticated enough to look past party labels. And D.C. voters certainly have in the past: In 1994, Carol Schwartz, a Republican member of the council, scored 42% of the vote against Marion Barry in the city’s mayoral race.

“Public safety, government accountability, taxes, and protecting our citizens are not just Republican or Democrat issues,” said Rivera. “They are D.C. residents’ issues.”

The main issue that animates almost all of the GOP contenders in D.C. is public safety — which has also been a primary focus of Trump’s, who last year deployed the National Guard in the city and frequently touts his successes on bringing down crime rates.
DC0A3210 copy.jpg (7403x4936, AR: 1.50)
“People don’t care if you’re from the left or the right. I tell them I am a Republican, that might jar them a bit, but I say, ‘Hey, what’s your biggest issue?’ And they say public safety,” said Jett Jasper, a candidate for the Ward 1 seat on the council, who says he would focus on increasing hiring for the Metropolitan Police Department.

Jorge Rice, who is running in Ward 6, says his emphasis on public safety comes from personal experience — he was assaulted on the D.C. streetcar in 2024, leaving him with a broken nose. “It made me want to take action,” he said.

In Ward 5, Jeff Kihien says it was rats in his backyard — as bipartisan a complaint as there is in D.C. — that motivated his own decision to run. “Washington D.C. is the capital of the United States, of the most powerful country on the whole planet, but we cannot solve the basic problem of rodents,” he said.

Kihien — who immigrated to the U.S. from Peru — also said he supports a “family wage” that would allow one half of every married couple to stay home instead of having to work.

Darrell Green, a former D.C. police officer who is running for an at-large council seat, is focused on one thing: “Education, education, education.” He thinks D.C. needs to do more to battle high truancy and absenteeism in schools. Abi Prudent, a candidate for council chair, is similarly interested in schools, primarily in preserving the IMPACT teacher assessment tool that some Democratic officials and activists have said they want to scrap.

“It’s hard for me to understand why we’d want to take away something that’s benefitting kids,” she said.

Denise Rosado, who is running to be D.C.’s non-voting delegate to Congress, would de-emphasize the city’s fight for statehood, instead pushing to exempt residents from paying federal taxes. As for Rivera, he criticizes incumbent Attorney General Brian Schwalb for “filing a lot of flashy lawsuits and some of them are settling for pennies on the dollar.”

‘The Hard Route’

The goal for the Republican candidates in D.C. seems clear: Don’t let Trump dominate the conversation. None of them fully shy away from Trump; they will say they voted for the president, but just as quickly point out where they disagree with him.

“It’s to the benefit of the voter you are talking about issues that you would have control over, and those are local issues like trash and recycling and rats and schools and the local budget,” said Carolina Celnik, the executive director of the D.C. GOP.

Still, there’s often significant overlap in D.C. between what happens on the local and federal levels — largely because the city is often beholden to the whims of Congress and the White House.

In that, the D.C. Republican Party has evolved over the years. It was once consistently in favor of Congress letting District residents and their elected officials determine their own fate; it even gave a nod towards the eventual goal of D.C. statehood. Now, Celnik says, local Republicans are content with the newly aggressive role that Capitol Hill is playing in local politics.

“They are doing what they are doing for the benefit of D.C. residents,” she said. “It’s honestly kind of embarrassing that the federal government has had to step in and do for the city what the city should have been doing for itself.”
DC0A2993 copy.jpg (6988x4659, AR: 1.50)D.C. voters, though, may disagree. A Washington Post poll conducted over the summer found that 79% of respondents said they opposed Trump’s aggressive involvement in local issues.

But given that the GOP has become so enmeshed in the city’s local affairs, the Republican candidates say they could serve as a friendly conduit between the White House, Congress and local officials.

“We should have a better relationship with the federal government and White House,” said Rivera. “As a Republican… I can build that bridge.”

Krucoff, the former Republican, thinks there is space for right-leaning candidates in D.C. Starting in 2028, independent voters — and there are roughly 80,000 of them — will be able to cast ballots in either the Republican or Democratic primary. That, he says, could open a path for a conservative contender while avoiding the political baggage of being associated with the GOP brand.

“It has never been a better time for anyone who sees themselves as center or right of center to become active in D.C. politics as an unaffiliated voter,” he said.

For D.C.’s local Republican candidates, though, the focus now is more pedestrian: They need to knock on doors and meet voters, as well as raise money. In that, another very real challenge emerges. As of last month, for one, Rivera had just over $10,000 in his campaign’s account. Schwalb, the Democratic incumbent, had $821,000. Prudent had roughly $2,300; Chairman Phil Mendelson, the incumbent, had $87,000.

Nonetheless, Prudent remains upbeat about the challenge she has assigned herself.

“Yes, I have allowed myself to take this campaign the hard route by running as a Republican,” she said. “But what’s most important for me is not trying to make things happen the easy way and trying to convince people to vote for me because of a letter that’s next to my name.”

entries.title: To Overhaul His Game, Frances Tiafoe Came Home
entries.summary: Tiafoe’s new routine included some hitting sessions with Ben Shelton, who he’ll face Friday in the U.S. Open semifinals.
entries.content:
Frances Tiafoe finished last season looking for a fresh start. It had been a decade since he turned pro, and despite flashes of brilliance and occasionally deep tournament runs, he’d found himself stalling and skidding through 2025. So he overhauled his approach. Tiafoe skipped most of the Asian and European competitions that round out the annual tennis calendar. He used the autumn to find a new coach and start a new practice regimen. And rather than relocating somewhere new or heading somewhere warm, Tiafoe instead went home to Maryland, training for roughly six weeks at the facility where he discovered the sport as a child in College Park, the Junior Tennis Champions Center.

He sometimes brought a very recognizable hitting partner.

Ben Shelton also spent time in the D.C. area this offseason. He is dating Washington Spirit star Trinity Rodman. Over the last few years on the ATP Tour, the 23-year-old Shelton and 28-year-old Tiafoe have been competitors, but they have grown into a friendship, too. It only made sense that, on multiple occasions, Shelton joined Tiafoe at JTCC.

The two elite talents mixed in with the ordinary hum of the surrounding courts. “It's a treat to have two players of that level, practicing in front of all of our kids and members,” says JTCC CEO Martin Blackman. “It was really special.”

The pair will play again this weekend on a somewhat bigger stage.

Friday night, Tiafoe and Shelton will meet in the U.S. Open semifinals. It will be their third time playing at the tournament in the last four years. (Shelton won in the quarterfinals in 2023; Tiafoe got revenge in the third round in 2024.) Each player is seeking his first Grand Slam final and, by extension, a chance to become the first American man to win a major since Andy Roddick in 2003. There will be a watch party, naturally, at JTCC.

Tiafoe and Shelton hit together at the facility at least three times as they prepped for this season, Blackman says. (JTCC posted a video of one such joint training session last November.) It was part of an unusually intense offseason at the facility for Tiafoe.

His relationship with the place has always been special. Nearly every match of his includes some commentary about his origin story and, in turn, his connection with JTCC: When he was a toddler, his father worked on the labor crew that built the facility, and that construction job became a maintenance role after the courts opened. From a young age, Tiafoe was surrounded by tennis, growing up around the facility and taking advantage of every opportunity he could find there. The son of Sierra Leonean immigrants became a prodigy and then a pro.

Like many tennis players, he established a base in Florida, where he generally spends his winters. But last offseason, searching for a way to shake up his career, Tiafoe decided that most of his training should happen back home in Maryland.
Frances Tiafoe (1956x1304, AR: 1.50)For years, Tiafoe had seemed perpetually on the verge of a breakthrough, always talented but never quite consistent. A strong run through 2023 and ’24 had faded into a lackluster 2025. He decided that something had to change. Tiafoe brought on a new coach, Mark Kovacs, with a focus on data and sports science.

“We all know he could play tennis at a high level,” Kovacs told the ATP Tour’s website in January. “Now it's about, ‘Can he take care of the little details on a daily basis?’” That meant everything from his fitness to his serve mechanics to his arrival time at the facility. (Kovacs is a stickler for punctuality.) They refined his diet and maximized his sleep. And on the same courts where he learned the game as a kid, Tiafoe worked to unlock a new level of performance as an adult.

“It was every day,” says Blackman, who originally worked at JTCC when Tiafoe was in elementary school and returned to run the center last year. “I mean, day in and day out.”

This was a striking change in approach for Tiafoe. It was immediately obvious in some ways: He lost 17 pounds. That kind of work does not always translate directly to better results on the court. Yet here it did. Tiafoe was in better shape, yes, but he was also more clear-minded about what he was chasing and it would ask of him.

“There’s a lot of things I've changed,” Tiafoe said at the French Open in May. “Just having a lot of conversations, trying to be real, man. What are you really trying to do? What are you trying to get out of it? You know, just stop hiding behind your talent, stop hiding behind the gift. … A lot of times you can get away with stuff because you're so gifted. But use the gift the right way, and, you know, squeeze a lemon and see what you can get out of it.”

Tiafoe began the season ranked No. 32. He now sits higher than ever at No. 8. He won his first ATP 500 trophy at the Terra Wortmann Open in June, and for just the second time in his career, has made it to at least the third round of all four Grand Slams. But his best performance of all has come over the last two weeks at the U.S. Open.

It has always been his favorite major — on home soil, in front of a traditionally loud, rambunctious crowd that matches his energy — and he has played like it.

Tiafoe cruised into the quarterfinals. He then dropped the first two sets to Alex Michelsen. It was a match that he might have easily lost a year ago — a match that nearly anyone would have lost at that point. Yet it was not a match that Tiafoe lost in 2026. He gutted out a remarkable comeback, winning 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (6), and promptly offered a touching display of sportsmanship by interrupting his own celebration to embrace a distraught Michelsen. That good cheer has always been a signature of his. But that particular brand of gritty, persistent tennis represented something new.

“The match against Michelsen, I think, is almost kind of the epitome of the difference in him now,” Blackman says. “He knows that as long as he’s in the match, he’s got a chance, because he’s always making adjustments, he’s fit enough to go the distance, and he’s got the belief that he can stand on the work that he did.”

Back at JTCC, where so much of that work took place, they were all watching. And they'll be watching again Friday night, as a familiar pairing faces off somewhere different.

entries.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates as Gas Prices Continue to Climb
entries.summary: The figures show that inflation remains stubbornly elevated, more than five years after prices first soared as the economy emerged from the COVID pandemic.
entries.content:
By Christopher Rugaber

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East, underscoring the affordability challenges that are top of mind for many voters with midterm elections now just seven weeks away.

The consumer price index rose 3.4% last month compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Friday, the same as in July. But on a monthly basis, inflation quickened, as costs jumped 0.4% from July to August, up from an increase of just 0.1% the previous month.

The figures show that inflation remains stubbornly elevated, more than five years after prices first soared as the economy emerged from the COVID pandemic. Persistent inflation has presented a major challenge for the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve and has soured many voters on the Trump administration’s economic track record.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices were 2.4% higher in August than a year ago, down slightly from July's 2.5% and the third straight decline. But on a monthly basis, core prices rose 0.3% from July to August, the largest increase since April.

The larger-than-expected monthly increase in core prices will likely embolden those Fed officials who have pushed for the central bank to lift its benchmark interest rate at its meeting next week. Wall Street investors now see about 70% likelihood the Fed will increase rates Sept. 16, according to CME Fedwatch.

The Trump administration is seeking to counter voter concerns about high prices and rising interest rates as the midterm elections approach. President Donald Trump on Wednesday promised $5,000 payments to every American adult if the GOP keeps a majority in Congress, a move that would require congressional approval and could stoke inflation. And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has stepped up buybacks of Treasury bonds in an effort to keep longer-term interest rates lower. Yet on Thursday the yield on the 10-year Treasury reached a nearly three-year high.

Renewed fighting in the Middle East has pushed up energy costs, with the nationwide average cost of a gallon of gas on Friday jumping more than 7% from a month ago to $4.30.

Hotel room prices and airfares also rose last month while new and used cars got more expensive. Apparel and grocery prices were unchanged from July to August.

Inflation as one-time shock, or something more

Many economists and Federal Reserve officials have long considered higher gas prices one of several “one-time” shocks that are lifting inflation, along with tariffs and surging investment in AI data centers. For months, the hope has been that as the war against Iran wound down, and the effects of tariffs faded, inflation would grind lower.

Yet there are few signs of the Iran war cooling, and even Trump has said gas prices won't retreat until after the midterm elections in November. And while Trump's trade fight with Canada will impact a small number of imports, it is a reminder that tariffs remain a threat that could push up other costs.

“This is not one and done,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. “It's unclear when tensions in the Middle East are going to settle down. ... This seems like it could be a prolonged disruption.”

While core prices are rising more slowly than overall prices, more expensive oil and gas could spread through more of the economy. Pricier jet fuel will likely push up airfares, and more expensive diesel will raise shipping costs, which could make groceries and other goods shipped by truck more expensive. On Thursday, a wholesale price report showed a jump in chemical prices, likely a result of more expensive oil.

What will the Federal Reserve do?

Federal Reserve policymakers are split on whether to hike at a meeting next week, so much so that differences of a few hundredths of a percentage point in Friday's inflation report could determine whether the central bank boosts its benchmark interest rate or leaves it unchanged. The Fed, which is tasked with keeping inflation in check, typically lifts borrowing costs to slow spending and limit price increases.

Investors and analysts differ over whether the Fed will hike rates at their Sept. 15-16 meeting. Chair Kevin Warsh suggested he was leaning toward a rate hike in a high-profile speech two weeks ago, but he did not commit to doing so at a specific time.

And last Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, echoing some other Fed officials, suggested that if Friday’s inflation report shows price increases cooling, then he would support keeping rates where they are. Waller is one of the 12 officials who vote on each Fed rate decision.

Waller's heavy emphasis on August's figures has raised the stakes for Friday's report. If the monthly core figure rounds up to 0.3%, some Wall Street analysts expect the Fed would then hike rates. But if it rounded down to 0.2% or lower, then a hold could be more likely. If it is somewhere in between, it's not clear what the Fed may do. One analyst called such considerations “ludicrous precision.”

For his part, Warsh doesn't want to tip his hand about his next moves, which some economists say will make this kind of uncertainty more common before Fed meetings.

entries.title: Why Swing District Republicans Kept Their Distance From Trump’s Midterm Convention
entries.summary: The GOP midterm convention in Dallas was a Trump-fest, and some imperiled Republicans thought it wasn’t worth the time.
entries.content:
DALLAS and BRIGHTON, Colorado — As the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention started on Wednesday afternoon at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, there were plenty of fervent supporters of President Donald Trump on hand, and plenty of Trump-themed merch.

Make America Great Again hats priced at $47 — a nod to the 47th president — shirts with the convention logo, cards sporting Trump’s face and more crowded the official souvenir stands for purchase by the faithful.

What was missing from the Trump-inspired scene were most of the people Trump said on Truth Social he wanted there — Republicans in competitive races.

Most of them stayed far, far away, in districts where vibes surrounding the unpopular president are far less positive. The convention presented a stark split screen, with Trump on one side calling for endangered members of Congress to join him amid the adoration and heated rhetoric of the MAGA base, while on the other side imperiled candidates aimed to soothe disenchanted locals.

One of those was Rep. Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who represents one of the state’s most competitive seats. He was about 800 miles northwest of Dallas as the convention launched, walking into a large conference room at the Electrical Independent Contractors of Rocky Mountain. He was attending a listening session with acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling to hear from the association’s board members.

“I might have considered going to it, you know? But at the end of the day, I'm going to be here in my community, listening to my community, taking care of my community,” Evans told The Washington Sun over a coffee at a local coffee shop in Brighton, Colorado.
Election 2026 Colorado (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)Trump reiterated his pitch to vulnerable Republicans in his prime-time keynote speech Wednesday night.

“You have so many of those great senators and I said, ‘You know the ones I want here, we have some that are leading by 30 points and they’ve been here for 25 years.’ I said, ‘Don’t come, please don’t come,’” Trump told the crowd. “The ones that we need are … the ones that are very close. They might be winning by a little or losing by a little, or tied.”

Evans and most other candidates facing similar circumstances did not answer the call. Of 70 speakers at the convention, only 18 were Republicans in tough House and Senate races. More than 40 Republican candidates and incumbents are considered to be tight races for seats in both chambers.

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the House Republicans’ campaign arm, which worked with the RNC to bring House lawmakers to Dallas, told The Sun that any concerns about the absence of vulnerable Republicans at the convention were just a “media kind of narrative about this, who's here, who's not here.”

“I just think it's D.C. trying to create some kind of narrative that there's some kind of disunity here. We're as unified as we've ever been, and this convention has been a great unifying focal point for us,” Hudson added.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Speaker Mike Johnson put a different spin on the divergent strategies of party leaders and their more reticent members: It’s just common sense, not evidence of a GOP divide.

“Anybody that wants to come and be a part of that is great. But we've also got members in tough races that want to be in their districts campaigning because they're literally going to win or lose by 1%. So some of them, you know, are in much better position being in their district,” Scalise told reporters.

Similarly, when asked last month while in New York whether he’d encourage members to go to the convention, Johnson said it “depends on the district.”

One House Republican in a competitive race who skipped the Dallas gathering and was granted anonymity to speak candidly, did not seem to have FOMO.

“I’m back in my district this week. Just finished knocking on doors for the night,” the lawmaker told The Sun via text Tuesday night.

When asked if the RNC, which organized the midterm convention, reached out about attending, the House Republican said, “I told them I would be working in the district and they left me alone.”

One person familiar with planning for the convention suggested that, despite what the president said, organizers didn’t actually want more lawmakers around, telling The Sun, “We want to actually have everyday Americans,” adding it’s “so much more powerful” than listening to “30 straight, 70-year-old dudes in a suit go up there and talk about policy.”

The priority for speakers, the person said, was those ordinary Americans first, followed by Cabinet members and, finally, vulnerable Republicans: “There’s only two nights, there’s only so many speaking slots, like, we can’t have everyone.”

Still, in a midterm when history favors the out-of-power party and Democrats are expecting a blue wave driven by Trump’s record-low approval ratings, an unpopular war in Iran, high gas prices and rising grocery costs, Evans was more interested in the everyday Americans back home.

“I'm taking care of my district,” Evans told The Sun.

“We did three site visits yesterday. People brought up new issues to me, and then I act on those issues,” Evans said “Whether it's writing letters, making calls, doing emails to the administration, talking to other members, I take care of my community and my neighborhood.”

Evans’ decision reflects the very precarious position he’s in. His seat, Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, is ranked a “toss up” by the Cook Political Report, with an even split between Republicans and Democrats.

Former President Joe Biden won the district by 5 percentage points in 2020. In 2024, Trump carried the district by just under 2 points, and his signature tough-on-immigration policies are a drag in the district.

Latino support has dropped significantly — recent polling found 61% of Latino voters there said they disapprove of the president, compared to 48% who disapproved of him in summer 2025.

“I am more conservative, and so I understand, I see both sides, but I'm also a human with empathy, and it's hard to watch,” said Febe Valdez, the owner of Willow and Fern, about the administration’s “harsh” mass deportation policies. “So I can't personally, can't really confidently say, I support violence and aggression when it comes to border control.”

For some, Trump's deportation tactics go beyond disapproval to hurting their pocketbooks.

Valerie Beltran, who owns Beltran’s Meat Market in Brighton with her husband, Cesar, blames the crackdown on migrants for driving down the couple’s sideline money-transfer business by 70%. Trump lauded the crackdown in his two-hour convention speech, but Beltran said it’s cost her income that covers most of the rent on their 5,600-square-foot building.

“I feel like it's the fear of sending their kids to school or coming to the Mexican markets to buy their produce or their meat, the shopping that they need to do daily supplies. Just fear of even leaving the house,” Beltran said. “That has contributed to the decline in sales.”

People who don’t go to markets also do not send money home to Mexico, Beltran said. She and her husband are among the many voters Evans has to worry about, though Evans has introduced a bill intended to shield some Latino businesses.

“The first time, I voted for Mr. Trump — both times. And the first time I was so happy. This time I'm not so happy, you know? I regret it this time,” Cesar said.

Those vulnerable Republicans who did attend the convention say there were benefits.

“Any time members of Congress or candidates have a national audience, that's an opportunity to talk about, especially as an incumbent, to talk about the things you've done in office,” Rep. Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania told The Sun.

Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, who took the stage Thursday night alongside the loved ones of individuals killed by undocumented immigrants, said he was “proud to stand with them and proud to fight for them.”

“Nobody has called me and said, ‘How dare you go to the convention?,’” Lawler said over the phone.

But for Evans, who’s in a district with a significant rural population, agriculture experts agreed he’d be better served by staying home.

“I would say anybody that represents a state that is undergoing as many pressures as they are back home in the district with the economic stuff for farms and ranches — if they can be there to support, probably not a terrible idea,” Kreg Vollmer, a state board member of the Colorado Farm Bureau, told The Sun.

“Personally, I would also prefer to stay in Colorado in August and not go to Dallas and die from the heatstroke. But that’s just me,” Vollmer joked.

Oriana González reported from Dallas. Kadia Goba reported from Brighton, Colorado

entries.title: Houthis Seize Territory in Another Key Strait, Complicating the Iran War
entries.summary: The Houthis’ biggest territorial gains in years, along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, could boost Iran’s strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States.
entries.content:
By Fatma Khaled, Samy Magdy and Cara Anna

CAIRO (AP) — Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured a strategic island at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, two officials said Friday, opening a new front in the Iran war and further threatening Saudi oil exports through one of the world’s key shipping lanes.

The Houthis’ biggest territorial gains in years, along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, could boost Iran’s strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States.

Saudi Arabia struck the airport in the nearby port city of Mokha that the Houthis seized Thursday, a Houthi broadcaster said. There were no reports of damage or deaths.

The capture of Mayun, a tiny, barren volcanic island inside the strait also known as Perim, was confirmed by a senior military official with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and by a Houthi official. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to journalists.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has increasingly relied on the Red Sea to get its crude to market as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been striking ships. Houthi moves to close the 28-kilometer-wide (17-mile) Bab el-Mandeb channel have made that route more complicated. Saudi officials declined a request by The Associated Press for comment on the developments.

In a statement Friday, the Houthi armed forces boasted of gains along the coast without mentioning the island, Mokha or the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They vowed “escalation for escalation” in the confrontation with Saudi Arabia, while declaring that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels.”

Still, markets are nervous, and experts have described the Houthis as highly unpredictable. Crude prices this week soared once again above $100 a barrel, giving Tehran more leverage in any talks.

Yemen's government shocked by slow Saudi response

The Houthis have been attacking Saudi shipping on the Red Sea since declaring a blockade in July, as well as oil infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia. The rebels said they acted in response to the kingdom’s yearslong blockade of Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

A senior military official with Yemen’s internationally recognized government told the AP they were stunned that the Saudi air force did not try to prevent the capture of Mokha, which is within 50 miles (80 kilometers) of the strait, by striking the Houthis as they advanced. He assessed that Saudi Arabia didn’t get a green light from the U.S. to embark on a large-scale air campaign.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t allowed to speak to the media, also blamed “lack of coordination” between Yemen’s army and multiple allied militias, saying it gave the Houthis “a priceless opportunity.”

Shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait had fallen by about 60% since the Houthis began attacking some ships there in late 2023 and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. Shipping increased this year as Saudi Arabia sought alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, but renewed Houthi threats have “curtailed” that activity, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence.

That has forced Saudi Arabia to find yet another alternative, sending its oil north out of the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, either via the Suez Canal or a pipeline through Egypt, a far longer route for its clients in Asia. The Houthis have threatened that route as well, striking a Saudi vessel in the north of the Red Sea in late August.

Iran calls for a return to Saudi-Houthi talks

Earlier Friday, Iran’s government called for an end to Saudi Arabia’s blockade of Houthi-held areas in a show of support for its ally. The Iranian Foreign Ministry also called for a return to negotiations between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

In a sign of how important the Houthis have become for Tehran, the spokesperson for Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard on Wednesday called for any negotiated settlement with the U.S. to include Yemen, the first explicit reference to that front. The call mirrored Iran’s past stance that a truce in Lebanon between its ally Hezbollah and Israel must be a part of any deal with the U.S.

Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also has said it has the right to defend itself in response to the Houthis’ blockade. The foreign ministers of Iran and Saudi Arabia spoke Thursday about diplomatic efforts to “restore stability” to the region, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on social media.

The fighting risks a return to Yemen's civil warAs the Houthis swept along the Red Sea coast toward the Bab el-Mandeb channel, Yemen’s Saudi-backed government called for international support.

In a statement Friday from a meeting the previous day, its National Defense Council said it was on the front line of defending freedom of navigation and condemned the Houthis’ renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen’s civil war since 2022. At stake are the 40 million people in the Arab world’s poorest country who fear a return to the conflict that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent over 46,000 people fleeing, the U.N. migration agency said Friday.

People seeking safety from the fighting are carrying few belongings, “whatever they can grab,” Abdusattor Esoev, chief of mission in Yemen for the International Organization for Migration, said in an interview Friday. He said the number of people displaced more than doubled this week and could still rise sharply.

“You see the fears in their eyes, and people are scared,” Esoev said.

The Houthis have been at war with Yemen’s government since 2014, when the rebels swept from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen, and the capital of Sanaa. Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on behalf of the government.

Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press Writer Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Judge Knocks Down Trump’s Order to Keep a Michigan Coal Plant Open
entries.summary: The federal circuit court said the Department of Energy’s interpretation of an “emergency” could threaten the stability of energy markets.
entries.content:
The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday shot down an effort from the Trump administration to keep a Michigan coal plant open past retirement.

The J.H. Campbell coal plant in West Olive, Michigan, just west of Grand Rapids, was scheduled to shut down last year. In preparation, the company that owns it worked to replace the facility with cleaner energy sources and had closure plans approved by state officials and grid authorities. But an emergency order from the Department of Energy directed the plant to continue running, using short-term federal emergency authorities.

The administration’s use of “emergency” authorities went too far, the federal judges wrote.

The Energy Department’s interpretation of an “emergency” would invite “frequent federal interventions” that could threaten the stability of the energy market, including by discouraging the development of new resources, Circuit court judges wrote in their decision.

The ruling could have larger implications for the Trump administration, which has used that same emergency authority to force several other coal plants to stay open in Pennsylvania, Indiana, Washington, Colorado and Florida. The Energy Department has re-issued those emergency orders as they expire every 90 days.

“The DOE needs to stay in its lane and use its emergency powers only in actual emergencies,” said Michael Lenoff, an attorney with Earthjustice, which petitioned the court to set aside the DOE’s order along with other advocacy groups. “Preventing the market-driven retirements of coal plants to advance a coal-friendly agenda is not a proper use of emergency powers.”

He said the group would continue to challenge those orders if the Trump administration continued to issue them.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Navy Leader Says Iran ‘Blew the Hell’ Out of the U.S. Base in Bahrain
entries.summary: Acting Secretary Hung Cao said this week that the Navy is weighing whether to repair the base that’s been rendered unusable.
entries.content:
The Navy is reconsidering the future of its Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain after Iranian attacks left the base badly damaged and unusable, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said this week.

“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” Cao told The Epoch Times in an interview Tuesday. Asked whether the Navy would repair the base, Cao said he has “a task force that’s looking at that.”

Naval Support Activity Bahrain is one of the most important U.S. military installations in the Middle East. It hosts the Fifth Fleet and U.S. Naval Forces Central Command, which oversee operations across the Persian Gulf, Red Sea and surrounding waters.

Iran repeatedly attacked the installation after the war began in February. The Pentagon initially said the strikes caused no U.S. deaths and did not significantly disrupt operations, but Navy officials have since acknowledged extensive damage.

Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told sailors last month that the Navy did not expect to return soon.

“We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” Caudle said at an Aug. 31 town hall. “I just want to be completely honest with that.”

The attacks damaged the Fifth Fleet headquarters, barracks, warehouses and communications infrastructure, according to The Wall Street Journal. Repairs could require roughly $400 million in construction.

The Navy has had to shift some logistics elsewhere in the region while the base remains out of service. Cao, whom President Donald Trump said earlier this month he would nominate to the position permanently, said the damage also left the USS Abraham Lincoln without the regional port and logistics hub normally available to a carrier operating in the Middle East.

The question of whether to rebuild the base comes as Iran is again stepping up attacks on U.S. forces.

Iran launched drones at U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sept. 1 during retaliation for another round of American strikes inside Iran. Bahrain said its forces intercepted the drones, and no major new damage to the U.S. base was reported.

Iran escalated further this week, firing about 20 ballistic missiles at a U.S.-used air base in Jordan after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. U.S. officials later acknowledged that several American combat aircraft were damaged in the attack.

Iran has also repeatedly targeted U.S. Navy ships as fighting around the Strait of Hormuz intensifies.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Officials Declare an End to the Record-Setting Cyclospora Outbreak
entries.summary: Its origin is still unknown.
entries.content:
By Mike Stobbe

NEW YORK — The largest cyclospora food poisoning outbreak in U.S. history is over, U.S. health officials said Friday.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration officials said they are confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific outbreak is off the market.

Nearly 13,000 reported cyclospora cases were tied to the multistate outbreak, federal officials say. They represent the bulk of an unprecedented surge in the parasitic diarrheal illness this year.

Even with the outbreak deemed over, several questions remain, including about its origin. The parasite is spread through human feces, and it still isn't clear how sewage could have contaminated enough food to sicken so many people.

“This contamination can happen if produce is grown in soil or comes into contact with water that has been contaminated,” said Ellen Shumaker, director of outreach for a North Carolina State University food safety program, Safe Plates.

Since May 1, the government has received reports of nearly 20,000 lab-confirmed cases, or more than 16 times the number reported during the same period last year. More than 6,100 suspected cases also have been reported.

The worst previous year in the U.S. for infections was 2019, when about 4,700 illnesses were reported nationally.

This year’s surge in cases was dominated by an outbreak in 21 states linked to iceberg lettuce. But there are thousands of other cases that have not been linked to that outbreak.

Michigan was the hardest hit state, with the most reported cases and the two U.S. deaths tied to the outbreak.

Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the CDC. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.

The illness, called cyclosporiasis, is less common than foodborne illnesses caused by other germs, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source.

In this outbreak, investigators initially zeroed in on lettuce served at Taco Bell. Federal officials subsequently focused on Taylor Farms as the source of the lettuce, and the company recalled iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico.

The Taylor Farms recall involved thousands of packaged salad products combining iceberg lettuce with other vegetables. The products were shipped to major U.S. restaurant chains, including Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, Pizza Hut and KFC.

The FDA has ended its on-site inspections and sample collection at iceberg lettuce growers and the processing facility in Mexico, the agency said Friday. Samples from the on-site inspections are pending analysis, the FDA said.

The outbreak cast a spotlight on a worsening problem: U.S. regulators are conducting fewer international inspections to catch contaminated produce before it lands on American plates.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: The DOJ Is Investigating the Clippers Over the Kawhi Leonard Scandal
entries.summary: The investigation stems from the NBA’s findings that the Clippers set up no-show endorsement deals for their star player to get around the league’s salary rules.
entries.content:
The Clippers’ salary cap circumvention scandal has made its way to the Justice Department.

On Thursday, The New York Times reported that federal prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation into the Clippers, related to the NBA’s findings that the team aimed to circumvent the league’s salary cap by setting up no-show endorsement deals for star Kawhi Leonard.

It isn’t known what crimes the Justice Department is investigating the Clippers for, according to the Times, or whether the investigation will result in charges.

The NBA released the findings of its investigation into the Clippers last week, while handing down one of the harshest penalties in league history. The investigation found that the team helped arrange four endorsement deals for Leonard with team sponsors that required little participation on his part, as a way to compensate him beyond his contract with the team and get around the league’s salary rules.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver stripped the Clippers of five first-round draft picks and suspended owner Steve Ballmer for a year, in addition to suspending two other team executives. Leonard must pay $700,000 in restitution, and Dennis Robertson, Leonard’s uncle and adviser, is banned from doing business in the NBA for five years.

Daktronics, which is one of the companies that made a deal with Leonard, is being probed by the Securities and Exchange Commission as a result of the NBA’s findings, the company’s CFO said on a recent earnings call.

According to the Times, the Justice Department’s investigation is being conducted by the U.S. attorney’s office in Brooklyn — which has a long history of investigating the NBA. In 2007, the office investigated former NBA referee Tim Donaghy, who bet on games he officiated and later served 15 months in prison, and in recent years the office has handled cases surrounding the federal gambling probe that led to the arrests of NBA players Terry Rozier and Malik Beasley as well as Trail Blazers coach Chauncey Billups.

After the NBA handed down its punishment, the Clippers issued a statement that said the team “vehemently reject the NBA’s findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence.” Ballmer’s attorney David Kelley, a former U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, released his own statement calling the investigation a “witch hunt,” but no mechanism exists within the NBA to challenge the league’s decision.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: GOP Congressional Candidate Backs Away From His 2020 ‘Stolen Election’ Claims
entries.summary: In an August debate, Ryan Elijah cast doubt on President Joe Biden’s victory in 2020. This week, he said he accepts the results.
entries.content:
Republican congressional hopeful Ryan Elijah, who defeated embattled Rep. Cory Mills in a bitter primary contest last month, backtracked this week on a series of previous claims he made about the 2020 election being stolen from President Donald Trump.

But when asked by local Florida TV station WKMG News 6 Wednesday if he thought the election was stolen, Elijah said, “No.”

“People would always ask me that and this is what I hear from Floridians: Look forward. That’s been six or seven years ago,” he continued.

It’s a sharp reversal from his previous stance on the election. While challenging Trump-endorsed Mills, Elijah walked a tightrope around the issue –– at a primary debate in August, Elijah said he did not “believe President Biden got more votes than Donald Trump in that race.”

But in the interview with WKMG, Elijah said that the question was intended to divide people, adding “Joe Biden was elected president and nobody is disputing that.”

Trump initially endorsed Mills but is supporting Elijah following his win in the primary. Mills has been dogged by multiple scandals, including a probe by the House Ethics Committee into allegations of sexual misconduct and campaign finance violations.

The Department of Justice is also investigating Mills’ finances. A list of prominent Florida Republicans, including fellow House members Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos, endorsed Elijah in the primary, citing Mills’ controversial past.

Elijah, a former news anchor in Orlando, won with 47% of the vote. But other Republicans were not as thrilled to see him flip-flop on the results of the 2020 election. Former Rep. George Santos wrote in a post on X Friday that he expects Elijah’s shift on that issue will be just the start.

“Y’all mad yet for voting for him instead of @CoryMillsFL?” Santos said. “This will be the biggest buyer’s remorse ever, just wait and see.”
entries.author: Avani Kalra

entries.title: U.S. Deports Afghan Woman Through a Newly Activated Secret Court
entries.summary: The Trump administration used the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time in its 30-year existence.
entries.content:
An Afghan woman living in Texas became the first person deported through a newly activated secret court last month, after a judge determined she fit the description of an “alien terrorist,” according to newly unsealed documents.

The FBI accused Nazira Haji Zada of being a radical Islamist who supported a plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting with her family, which had relocated to the United States after her husband assisted the U.S. war effort back in their home country. The Justice Department in July activated the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time in the court’s 30-year existence to seek her removal from the U.S.

She was not charged with a crime, but investigators said that she helped her son and son-in-law plan an attack during the 2024 general election — one that turned out to be a federal sting operation.

U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen of Minnesota — one of five jurists on the terrorist removal court — issued an order on Aug. 20 that stripped Haji Zada of her American residency status, deemed her “an alien terrorist,” deported her to Afghanistan and rendered her permanently inadmissible to the United States.

She was deported five days later, according to a court filing by prosecutors. Haji Zada, through her federal defender attorney, conceded to her removal on the condition that the accusations not be used against her in a criminal case.

The documents were unsealed Thursday but posted on Friday, as the nation observed the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Her removal from the country shows how the Justice Department could use the terrorist removal court to brand someone a terrorist without affording them the opportunity to view the evidence the government claims to have against them.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement, called it a “landmark case” and added that “the ATRC shows how the [DOJ] will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country.” FBI Director Kash Patel issued a statement saying that federal law enforcement is now “using all means necessary” to protect the country from the threat of terrorism.

The ATRC, which was created by Congress in 1996, remained dormant until this year. Its existence and method of operation — unlike a typical criminal court, it doesn’t need to follow due process laws — worry legal experts who have called its constitutionality into question.

Alfred Wolin, the only living jurist who was among the first batch of judges to sit on the court, told The Washington Sun earlier this summer that even he was confused about how exactly the process would work.

Haji Zada spent several weeks listed as “Inmate 400151” at a D.C. jail as the case proceeded largely behind closed doors.

Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were previously convicted of charges related to the planned attack. Her son was 17 at the time of his arrest in 2024 and is currently listed as an inmate at a medium-security federal prison in California, with an expected release date in 2037. Tawhedi pleaded guilty last year but has not yet been sentenced.

This case also included the State Department, immigration enforcement, and the DOJ’s National Security Division to coordinate the deportation.
entries.author: Jose Pagliery

entries.title: Trump Commemorates the 25th Anniversary of 9/11 in Subdued Pentagon Speech
entries.summary: It's the second year in a row Trump marked the day at the Pentagon.
entries.content:
By Collin Binkley, Aamer Madhani and Meg Kinnard

President Donald Trump observed Friday’s 25th anniversary by speaking about the Sept. 11 attacks at a ceremony at the Pentagon commemorating the lives lost when al-Qaida militants hijacked planes and killed nearly 3,000 people in three locations, upending American foreign policy and national security.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump listened as the names of the 184 people killed at the Pentagon that day were read aloud, a bell tolling between each. In his remarks, Trump recounted the stories of several of the victims. “We will never, ever forget,” Trump said. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice.”

Earlier, in a downpour at daybreak, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and top military officials stood outside and watched as a giant American flag was unfurled on the building struck by one of those planes a quarter- century ago.

It's the second year in a row for Trump to mark the day at the Pentagon. The president, who is originally from New York, last attended the ground zero ceremony there in 2024.

Vice President JD Vance is attending the New York observance alongside former presidents, while other administration officials are at the ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Vance had planned to be in New York for the anniversary last year but instead flew to Salt Lake City to be with the family of Charlie Kirk after the conservative activist was assassinated.

Trump began his remarks by recalling the sense of American unity following the attacks. “In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation,” Trump said. “We were all New Yorkers that day. Every one of us. We were all New Yorkers. We were all family.”

The president and his defense secretary sought to connect the events of 9/11 to the war with Iran. Trump saluted the service members “working right now to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of terror — the Islamic Republic of Iran — will never, ever have a nuclear weapon.”

Hegseth said the U.S. military had “laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism." He added: “Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11, a regime that has sponsored terrorist attacks against Americans for decades, killing thousands, including our comrades in Iraq, in Afghanistan.”
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Talarico Calls Kimmel Interview Drama the ‘Most Dangerous Form of Cancel Culture’
entries.summary: Jimmy Kimmel said ongoing threats from the FCC led ABC not to air the interview on television.
entries.content:
Texas Senate candidate James Talarico decried ABC’s decision to not air an interview he sat for on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” as “the most dangerous form of cancel culture,” while assailing the Trump administration for pressuring the network to alter its programming.

Talarico addressed the circumstances surrounding his interview with Kimmel on Thursday, telling MS NOW that “government censorship should be a concern to all of us, regardless of our political party.”

“I think it’s the most dangerous form of cancel culture,” Talarico said. “People at the top — powerful politicians, powerful media executives — censoring what we watch, what we read, what we say. That should be a concern to everyone who believes in the First Amendment and believes in the freedom of speech.”

Kimmel posted the full interview to YouTube late Thursday night. He asked the Texas state representative about religion, his opponent Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and voter suppression.

When Kimmel asked Talarico why the administration was so keen to get him off the air, Talarico answered, “They’re worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas.”

ABC has faced ongoing threats from the Federal Communications Commission and its chair, Brendan Carr, over workplace diversity practices, Talarico’s appearance on daytime talk show “The View,” and for remarks Kimmel made in September 2025 after the conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s death, which resulted in a brief suspension of his show.

After the FCC signaled it would review the broadcast licenses of ABC’s owned and operated television stations years before they were set to expire, ABC accused the commission in a regulatory filing of retaliation. ABC and its parent company Disney sued the FCC on Aug. 18 over accusations that its First Amendment rights were being violated.

In February, an interview between Talarico and Stephen Colbert, who hosted a late-night show on CBS up until this spring, was also uploaded to YouTube due to the FCC’s enforcement of the “equal time” rule, which dictates that radio and TV broadcasters must provide equal airtime to competing political candidates if requested.

Kimmel titled his interview with Talarico “Jimmy Kimmel’s Interview with James Talarico That the FCC Doesn’t Want You To See” and began the conversation by saying the FCC has issued threats against him, his show, ABC and its affiliates because “they want to make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept.”

That was why, Kimmel said, the interview would be posted on YouTube, “even though our government would clearly prefer that we not do it at all.”

Kimmel also said he would “love” to interview Paxton in accordance with the FCC’s “equal time” rule, saying he had a lot of questions for the Republican candidate.“Call me,” Kimmel said to Paxton at the end of the segment.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic Researcher Who Quit, Explains Why Now
entries.summary: Being a sci-fi lover led Coxon to work on artificial intelligence. The culture of the industry left him “a bit hopeless.”
entries.content:
Within 48 hours, Jacob Coxon had been mocked by billionaire Elon Musk, reposted by Sen. Bernie Sanders, and inundated by calls from government officials, reporters and the tech world.

The 27-year-old British researcher quit Anthropic on Tuesday with an urgent warning that the race between the giants of artificial intelligence was at risk of spiraling out of control. His subsequent thread on social media cautioning that Anthropic and OpenAI are speeding toward “superintelligence” — a theorized point at which AIs far surpass human capabilities — without adequate safeguards, received more than 160 million views. It has been widely seen as a watershed moment in altering the public’s awareness about the fears within the AI labs of the dangers of their models.

“The actual work just felt like I'm just contributing to the potential death race, and there's a lot of talk about ‘mutual slowing down’ — but everyone has still got their heads down, just going as fast as they can,” Coxon said in an interview with The Washington Sun.

The dizzying improvements of new models from both companies in the past few months, combined with a string of hacks in which the AIs defied human instructions, have magnified the concerns of safety researchers both inside and outside the two firms.

Coxon worked at OpenAI for three years, starting in 2023, before joining Anthropic earlier this year. During his time in the industry, Coxon found that the pressure to “maintain revenue and keep being competitive” often prevailed over concerns among engineers about safety.

Not everyone has agreed with Coxon’s criticisms. Musk claimed that Coxon's post "seems like a setup” as part of the “doomer” community — the online subculture of extreme nihilism and pessimism. Forbes wrote that Coxon's post was "vague, with no proof, and no specific examples that are easy for the public — and regulators — to act on." Other tech boosters have pointed to Coxon’s relatively short tenure at Anthropic.

In an interview, Coxon explained his decision to quit, argued for international cooperation between the U.S. and China, and explained why he remains optimistic that effective regulation is possible.

This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

Stein: I wanted to start by asking a little about you. How do you get into this world, what’s your way in, and what drew you to AI?

Coxon: I'm from the UK — Oxford. My favorite science fiction has always included “Permutation City” by Greg Egan, a story essentially about entering a simulation. I've also always liked Iain Banks' Culture novels, which portray AI done well — a future where we're surrounded by superintelligent AI that generally acts in our favor.

Like a lot of nerdy kids, I read a lot of sci-fi. AlphaGo happened in 2016, when I was in high school. [AlphaGo is a computer program that beat advanced human professionals at the game Go in March 2016.] It was a very exciting moment. At that point, the idea was we'd scale up games and make them more and more realistic — the world as a game — and that was how we'd get to AI. But the real turning point came later, with ChatGPT-3 — the realization you could get there just by modeling language.

I think the technology is inherently very exciting. To me, it could unlock research advancements in every field, and in particular in maths. My previous area was as a maths undergrad and I was considering doing research in maths. Maths is also inherently interesting, but there's also all this tedious work — and there's very obvious benefits of automating tedious work.

It's this double-edged sword in that it is just so tempting — the idea of being able to just blast through new areas of maths, for instance, but also this fear of what it would look like. It's this enticing, tempting technology where you're kind of aware it's got this upside and it's got this downside, in that it will change everything and potentially render the whole discipline meaningless.

And, obviously, this idea of just being able to solve diseases before me and my parents get old — that would be very nice. I still think there's every possibility that something like that is in the cards.

Stein: When you first got to OpenAI in 2023, did that sense of potential feel like it was being confirmed?

Coxon: When I joined, the long-term goals still felt like science fiction and felt like a long way out — sufficiently distant that it didn't really interfere that much with the present-day work. It's like there's this nebulous future possibility of a big thing that also leads to a ton of funding and interest, and also is a motivating fact for people working on it.

But it was, at least in the past, harder to bring that to bear on the day-to-day. The day-to-day felt like we were still just writing code, training models. They were maybe getting better at certain tasks, but it felt very different from the big sci-fi thing of the future.

Stein: When did that start to change, even for the first time?

Coxon: So it starts to change probably with the rise of people using coding agents — that was one big thing. And then for me personally, seeing the mathematics results has been pretty insane, especially with also my friends that are still doing math, seeing AI knock out Navier-Stokes in quite a short period of time on a new model — that is pretty ridiculous. This was the Millennium Prize Problem.

And then on a practical day-to-day level, once you get to the stage where it's now, you're just talking to these AIs. They’re helping do your research. You're asking them their opinions on your research. You're asking them to go and do experiments for you to report back to other AIs, to go and collaborate with each other, maybe try spinning up some runs, improving their own code, and then this is just a part of daily reality.

This really became part of reality this year, and that I think was another big step towards the big future, AI becoming relevant for daily work and feeling tied up with daily work.

Stein: So, can you walk me through the decision to leave OpenAI and go to Anthropic? I know you've talked about it a little bit, but I would love a little bit more about the decision points there.

Coxon: While I was there, OpenAI was lacking a lot of the internal communications about the future of AI. Which has two effects. It's maybe bad in terms of preparing people for what's coming — but it also makes the place feel sane and kind of safe, which makes it a lot harder to get very scared about the future.

But I had lots of friends at Anthropic, and I was very curious to see if their internal culture matched what they were publicly presenting. Because they're a lot more closed off than OpenAI and it’s very hard to tell what their overall perspective is, how likely things are — they keep their cards very close to their chest. But also internally, they're much more open about this sort of stuff.

Fortunately, OpenAI culture has changed in the last couple months; people became a lot more scared after things like the Hugging Face attack. But comparing my experience at the two places, the move was definitely vindicated in terms of getting a better perspective about what people honestly, concretely thought about stuff.

Stein: So if Anthropic was safer, what did you see there that led you to quit so suddenly?

Coxon: Arriving was basically just a confirmation that people were being very open about their opinions about stuff. There was also a realization that alignment's [the industry term for ensuring AI "aligns" with ethical preferences] not solved yet. Anthropic is definitely — at least while I was at both companies — they're taking it very seriously as an institution, compared to OpenAI. I think there is no way Anthropic would have let the Hugging Face message board carry on after they first discovered it, which is what I understand happened at OpenAI.

At the same time, at both companies there's pressure: to launch new models; to get recursive learning training going fast; to start new forms of training. There's a lot of pressure to test them out, especially if you think other companies are doing them.

For example, OpenAI swarm behavior [when AI “agents” coordinate together on solving tasks]. There's clearly pressure on both sides to try and think about how to run these multi-agent systems and clearly do so before very rigorously laying out a case for alignment. So it became pretty clear that in the context of the race, both OpenAI and Anthropic, no matter how seriously they're taking it, would be forced to make innovations very quickly, potentially leaving rough edges.

Rough edges right now are kind of fine. They'll just lead to things like a hack or weird corner-cutting behavior. But rough edges in a year or two with a very intelligent model — that's very scary.

They have to discuss: “Should we launch a model on X date with these risks?” Or, “Should we push the launch two weeks, delay it for these reasons?” And there's the pressure of staying on the frontier, which is required to maintain revenue and keep being competitive and keep being the one that's in the lead, versus the pressure that delaying releases creates for the sake of making sure that every little thing is covered.

I want to reiterate: This is not, at the moment, like Anthropic is cutting corners with its biosafeguards or its cyber safeguards. They are doing those to the utmost capability — that is not a thing they are trying to skimp on. This is cutting corners on things that could lead to some problems, but are not now existential.

The real risk is everything becomes existential when your model is really smart. I was working on capabilities and pretraining research at Anthropic and was gradually becoming more concerned with the state of the race. I switched to working on safety for about one week, and I moved to a safeguards team. But I found that when I made the switch it felt a bit hopeless; I still had all the same feelings about imminent disaster.

It really wasn't about the nature of the work. It was more like the sense that something needed to happen with regard to actually making a slowdown happen soon. The actual work just felt like I'm just contributing to the potential death race, and there's a lot of talk about mutual slowing down — but everyone has still got their heads down, just going as fast as they can.

Stein: How far off do you think we are from that? And when will average people start noticing the effects of this in their day-to-day lives?

Coxon: There's a lot of different factors here. One thing that could be very tangible pretty soon is if many models, including open-source models, reach the current level of hacking capabilities, which could happen potentially before you see the real downstream effects of recursive self-improvements.

I think probably in the immediate future, if the labs kind of get their shit together with regard to control and monitorability, which it seems like they're doing, then the biggest thing the public might expect is major hacks from open-source models, or from models that are not being observed as well as the big lab models.

And then after that, I think what's so scary about this is in the cases where our monitorability of these systems is good, you don't really get much of a warning for the thing that's very smart, smart enough to evade your monitor systems, and then the sort of damage it causes could look very visceral. So the thing that sounds kind of scary, science fiction — and a little bit fake about this is — in the worst case scenario, you don't really get a warning until it's sort of at a level of intelligence where it's betraying you.

I think one thing that you could also expect to see is way more reports of people within the labs doing this sort of research, where they attempt to prove that this sort of thing is possible. But then, what that looks like from the outside for the public is people releasing articles saying stuff like, “Scientists working in these labs say they lost containment.” And the typical response to that has been and probably will be just like, “Oh, it's just some scientists hyping up their own products or hyping up their own stock” — that’s kind of what people see. But I think you could definitely expect to see more of that, at least before you get the actual deception.

Stein: I know the most important thing you want to convey is the urgency of the collective action problem. What do you think policymakers need to do? And could you address the China question — the argument that if the U.S. slows down, it just lets China develop less-controlled open models with the same risks?

Coxon: I don't know the details of international relations. I'm hopeful that the people building this technology in China will realize they're facing the same problem we are. I was having a discussion earlier where someone made the analogy that it's not really the U.S. versus China — it's more like the U.S. and China are both facing contact with an alien species, and there's a choice between fighting each other to build stronger aliens on our respective sides versus banding together against the aliens.

I'm sure that obscures a lot of detail about what negotiations would actually look like, but my gut feeling is we should be able to agree this technology could be very dangerous. All I know is the current race poses significant risk. One of the main arguments my Anthropic colleagues who stay make is that they're pessimistic about the actual possibility of international coordination — they expect the race to happen regardless, and so they'd rather be the ones making sure it goes well.

I just think that if you're going to accept a 10% chance of catastrophic risk because you're racing with China, you should check really, really hard that there's no deal to be made instead.

Stein: But does it matter whether it’s carefully controlled or not? Are we screwed either way once we get to recursive self-improvement because then the AIs will just invariably improve on their own?

Coxon: No, it can happen. Recursive self-improvement could be done safely if you have consistent human oversight, you're constantly aware of what's going on, and you're confident you've gotten it right. It would have to happen slowly. I can't speak exactly to what the government should do — government regulation is pretty scary in itself. I think the minimal thing is that labs need some kind of agreed-upon capability to slow down.

There are a lot of proposals for this — a pretty obvious one is being completely transparent about how close you are to recursive self-improvement, and agreeing not to proceed until certain transparent safety conditions are met, like a rigorous, audited safety case. But you also need the same thing applied internationally, which is the really hard part — there can't just be a private handshake deal between Western labs.

You need international recognition that entering recursive self-improvement has to be done collectively. That’s what has to happen.

entries.title: George W. Bush Paints the Moment He Was Told About 9/11
entries.summary: It’s part of a new collection of works by the former president.
entries.content:
Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks that defined his presidency, George W. Bush is revisiting the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, through paintings.

Bush has created a new series commemorating 9/11, depicting scenes and people connected to the attacks and their aftermath. The collection, “Remembering 9/11,” is on display at the George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum in Dallas through the end of September.

For Bush, the memories of that morning are particularly vivid.

He was visiting Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida, where he was reading "The Pet Goat” to a classroom of second graders, when then-White House chief of staff Andrew Card leaned over and whispered to him: “A second plane hit the second tower. America is under attack.”

The moment was captured in photographs that became some of the defining images of the day. Bush remained seated for several moments before leaving the classroom and beginning to respond to the attacks. He would eventually address the nation, be moved to several secure locations and return to Washington that evening.

The attacks ultimately shaped Bush’s presidency, leading to the war in Afghanistan, the invasion of Iraq and a sweeping expansion of the U.S. government’s counterterrorism policies.

But in retirement, Bush has increasingly revisited the people affected by those wars through a different medium — painting.

Bush took up painting after leaving the White House in 2009, inspired in part by Winston Churchill’s essay “Painting as a Pastime.” What began as a hobby became a significant part of his post-presidential life. He has painted portraits of veterans, immigrants, world leaders, family members, pets and himself.

His 2017 book, “Portraits of Courage,” featured paintings and stories of wounded U.S. service members who served in the wars that began during his presidency. Bush has said the project was intended to highlight the sacrifices and resilience of veterans.

Now, his paintings are bringing him back to the event that changed the course of his presidency — and the country.

The new collection focuses on the courage, sacrifice and resilience that emerged from 9/11, according to the Bush Center.

While former presidents and New York politicians gathered at the World Trade Center to memorialize the 25th anniversary of 9/11, President Donald Trump oversaw the anniversary at the Pentagon this morning. He and Pete Hegseth sought to connect the events to the ongoing Iran war, thanking service members for working to ensure “the world’s No. 1 sponsor of terror — the Islamic Republic of Iran” can’t develop a nuclear weapon.

The contractor who renovated the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool told the Trump administration that errors in its own work — not vandalism — had caused the feature’s blue liner to break loose.

Swing district Republicans kept their distance from this week’s midterm convention.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) failed to properly submit an annual report detailing his billion-dollar personal fortune, blowing past a legal deadline despite requesting and receiving two extensions, The Sun’s Mark Alfred found.

The DOJ is investigating the Los Angeles Clippers’ salary cap circumvention scandal.

The EPA is proposing to drastically weaken environmental restrictions on oil and gas wells that produce little energy but release vast amounts of methane, ProPublica reports.

The CIA released dozens of intelligence documents it sent to Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush in the months and years before the 9/11 attacks, The New York Times reports.

A federal appeals court blocked the Trump administration’s effort to keep a Michigan coal plant open past retirement.

The Texas Supreme Court knocked down implementation of a Galveston County redistricting plan officials adopted after the state’s March primaries, saying it cannot be used in November.
