entries.title: Republicans Jump at the Chance to Advertise on Trump’s $5,000 Checks
entries.summary: The president proposed a vague plan to distribute payments if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate in November.
entries.content:
Republican incumbents and candidates are already fundraising around President Donald Trump’s undetailed promise to send $5,000 checks out to Americans if Republicans keep control of both the House and the Senate in the November midterms.

Groups affiliated with Reps. Wesley Hunt of Texas and Jimmy Patronis of Florida sent fundraising emails based on the check on Thursday and Friday, featuring messages like: “Trump just promised $5,000 back in your pocket if Republicans hold Congress this midterm. … This is your FINAL CHANCE.”

Challengers across the country are deploying a similar tactic. A campaign text promoting Eric Flores — a Texas Republican running in what the Cook Political Report has deemed a “toss up” race against Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez — also touted Trump’s proposal in a message to potential voters.

“Attachment: $5,000 check for Mr./Mrs. [BLANK]. Pres. Trump just authorized it. Access portal & support approval ASAP,” the text reads before linking to Flores’ WinRed fundraising page.

In New Hampshire, House candidate Anthony DiLorenzo’s campaign in a lean-Democrat district sent an email stating “IF YOU” help Republicans win the midterm elections, “THEN TRUMP will send you a $5,000 Trump dividend check! Deal or no deal?”

Other Republican campaigns in Democrat-leaning states and districts, including Rosie Pino’s House campaign in New Jersey and Bert Mizusawa’s Senate campaign in Virginia, sent fundraising emails with similar motifs soon after Trump’s announcement.

None of the campaigns responded immediately to a request for comment.

Trump’s campaign also blasted several fundraising emails, as did the Senate Patriot PAC, a group that supports electing Republican senators.

“Would you want a $5,000 check thanks to me, TRUMP, if we win BOTH the House of Representatives and the United States Senate?” one email reads.

Many Republican lawmakers have cast doubt on the feasibility of Trump’s idea, which he announced on stage at Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas. More than a dozen lawmakers, aides and policy experts told The Washington Sun on Thursday that they were blindsided by the announcement, with one person briefed on the pledge describing the planning as “not very vigorous.”

A handful of GOP lawmakers and executive branch members have offered tentative proposals on how the president could distribute around $1.2 trillion in dividends to American adults, though Trump himself has not laid out clear plans.

Retiring Republican Rep. Ralph Norman of South Carolina poured cold water on the proposal on Friday, saying that he has “serious concerns” about “another massive spending package without a clear way to pay for it.”

“Tying government checks to the outcome of an election starts to sound like pay-to-play politics,” he wrote in a post on X. “Republicans should earn the support of the American people through good policy, not by promising another round of checks from Washington.”

entries.title: Contractor Admitted That Human Error Caused Reflecting Pool Damage
entries.summary: An August report reviewed by The New York Times revealed contractors told the administration that its own mistakes caused the pool floor to blister.
entries.content:
Contractors working on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation told the Trump administration that its own mistakes — not vandalism — damaged the pool’s liner, new documents reveal.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings detailed the cause of the pool’s eventual swampy appearance in Aug. 14 reports to the government, The New York Times first reported on Friday. Workers had mistakenly layered two incompatible chemicals that caused paint on the pool liner to blister and peel, and some areas were not covered with enough primer to keep the paint job intact, the report said.

The documents reviewed by the Times, which also included daily progress updates from the National Park Service, show that the government had knowledge that human error caused at least some damage, even as they pursued criminal vandalism charges at President Donald Trump’s request. While the report shows that Atlantic blamed vandals for cuts in the pool’s edge caulking, the company did not link those incidents to the liner peeling.

The Justice Department abruptly dropped a criminal case against former U.S. Olympian David Hearn earlier this year after he was accused of purposefully vandalizing the pool. In its filing, prosecutors admitted that the damage had stemmed from “flawed installation by the contractor.” This came after administration officials, including Trump and U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, maintained for months that vandals were responsible for the pool’s damage.

At an August news conference held days before Atlantic’s full report to the government, Trump acknowledged contractor error, but continued to claim damage from vandalism was “substantial.”

"Unfortunately,” he said on Aug. 10, “there is no video or proof, other than the damage itself."

The administration has otherwise been quiet on the issue since last month, including after Trump remarked that Pirro had “folded like an umbrella” after she dropped the charges against Hearn. Pirro, Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum had a contentious meeting in which Pirro blamed Burgum for misleading the president about what the evidence suggested.

On Wednesday, Pirro declined to answer a reporter's question about her office's now-dropped vandalism case.

"No, no and no!" she said. "Who wants to know about this? How many times do I have to say no? I am not talking about that."

In a statement to The Washington Sun, an Interior Department spokesperson maintained that sections of the pool were damaged by vandals, and added that the administration is still “cleaning up Obama’s and Biden’s mess.”

“Like any major construction project — and in this case, the world’s largest reflecting pool which was worked on in record time for the 250th celebrations — there are always parts of a project where a contractor returns to make sure the work is perfect,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.

The Parks Service brought back Atlantic, which won a no-bid contract to carry out the initial repairs, to complete additional repairs. The reflecting pool will soon be opened with new “American Flag blue” paint, repaired plumbing, shiny granite coping stones and a brand new water treatment system, the spokesperson said.

“[Atlantic] is contractually obligated to fix the Reflecting Pool,” the spokesperson said. “As good stewards of taxpayer money, unlike Obama, it would be wasteful to bring in a new company to finish the job.”

The White House did not address the contractor’s report when approached by The Washington Sun.

“For years, the Reflecting Pool sat neglected, plagued with algae, and leaking millions of gallons of water. Fixing it was common sense. It’s another example of President Trump restoring our nation’s capital for the American people,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in an email.

entries.title: Two Former DHS Chiefs Call for an Agencywide ‘Reset’
entries.summary: Under the Trump administration, the department has diverted a large segment of its resources toward immigration enforcement and domestic operations.
entries.content:
Two former Cabinet secretaries called for the federal government to “rethink and reimagine” the Department of Homeland Security, arguing that it may be abandoning its counterterrorism efforts as President Donald Trump reshapes the agency to carry out his immigration crackdown.

Michael Chertoff and Jeh Johnson, who served as DHS secretaries under presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama, respectively, said in a joint interview with NBC News Thursday that the federal government must pursue a balance between enforcing domestic immigration laws and protecting the country from threats.

“I get concerned sometimes when I think that we’re spending most of our time worrying about gardeners and home health aides and getting them thrown out of the country, as opposed to focusing on people that actually are doing a lot of damage,” Chertoff said.

The Trump administration has redirected a massive amount of resources toward immigration and deportation operations, including State Department funds for countering foreign election interference and a DHS budget focused on weapons of mass destruction. Former DHS officials and Democratic lawmakers have said the massive boost toward immigration enforcement is deviating the department from Congress’ original intention.

Johnson added in the interview that the Trump administration’s laser focus on immigration has become “more than a distraction.”

“I think it has overwhelmed the Department of Homeland Security,” he said. “I fear in many communities DHS has become a pariah, radioactive, the department of mass deportations, heartless, locking up kids, and that is one of the reasons why I think we need a reset.”

The department said in a statement to The Washington Sun that its focus on immigration only served to bolster its counterterrorism operations and blamed former President Joe Biden for endangering public safety through lax immigration enforcement.

“Counterterrorism and immigration enforcement go hand in hand,” the statement said. “Child exploitation, trafficking, terrorism, scams, and smuggling all have a nexus to illegal immigration.”

Bush established DHS through passage of the Homeland Security Act in 2002, following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The law unified 22 federal departments and agencies into one Cabinet agency, largely emphasizing in its language that the goal was to “prevent terrorist attacks within the United States.”

Chertoff acknowledged that technology has drastically changed in the last few decades, which has provided greater capabilities to detect explosives or other weapons being brought onto a plane. Johnson said that terrorist threats have also evolved since then, too, and questioned whether DHS was in a position to navigate those changes.

“I always tell people,” Johnson said, “you’re safe until the moment you’re not.”

entries.title: Sen. Jim Justice Failed to Properly Disclose His Massive Wealth
entries.summary: The West Virginia Republican — a billionaire — blew past a federal transparency deadline.
entries.content:
Sen. Jim Justice failed to properly submit an annual report detailing his billion-dollar personal fortune, blowing past a legal deadline despite requesting and receiving two extensions, The Washington Sun found.

Justice filed his annual financial disclosure on Tuesday, about a month past an Aug. 13 deadline mandated by the Ethics in Government Act.

The West Virginia Republican is the richest man in the Senate, with assets of about $1 billion — and possibly much more — mostly owed to his coal-mining enterprises. Justice regularly flies back and forth from Washington via private jet.

Senators, including Justice, are required by law to annually disclose their assets, liabilities and sources of income. Lawmakers need only disclose their assets’ value in ranges, and Justice’s disclosure includes over a dozen line items valued at “over $50,000,000,” making it impossible to nail down his exact net worth.

Justice’s office did not return a request for comment.

Justice’s tardy report, which covers financial activity during 2025, is similar to his previous annual disclosure from 2024: Justice continues to be extremely wealthy and maintains his various mining and energy assets as well as a surgery center and a golf and tennis club.

One line item from his earlier filing labeled “Blind Trust of James C Justice, II” that was valued at “over $50,000,000” isn’t included in Justice’s latest disclosure.

Justice’s latest report indicates his liabilities have grown by as little as $25.8 million and as much as $120 million during the past year.

Lexon Insurance Company sued Justice over “unpaid premiums and collateral owed on surety bonds” related to his coal mining businesses. The company was granted nearly $30 million in damages late last year.

Justice’s potential penalty for improperly disclosing his personal finances is decidedly more manageable: He faces a $200 fine, which the Senate Ethics Committee can choose to waive. The committee did not respond to a request for comment.

Justice joins an ever-growing list of federal lawmakers who’ve violated the Ethics in Government Act or the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act by failing to properly disclose their personal finances.

Since last summer, violators in the House include Reps. Gil Cisneros (D-California), Michael Rulli (R-Ohio), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Tracey Mann (R-Kansas), Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Derek Tran (D-California), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

Senators who’ve violated the STOCK Act during the past year include Sens. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

entries.title: Husted Fires Political Director Over Past Nazi Posts
entries.summary: The former staffer had posted profile photos featuring Nazi officers and wore the attire in a group photo in 2018.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Husted fired his campaign’s political director Friday after discovering the staffer had posted Nazi imagery on social media and made playlists of songs celebrating Rhodesia, an unrecognized south African state often touted by white supremacists.

Stephen Woytek, who joined the Ohio Republican’s campaign last month, had posted profile photos depicting Nazi officers on his Facebook page and published links to a military reenactment group whose members dress up as Nazi officers. Woytek himself is pictured wearing the attire with the members of the group in photos from 2018, when he was 16 years old, according to The Washington Post, which first reported the social media activity earlier Friday.

A campaign spokesperson described Woytek as a “lieutenant in the U.S. Army” who studies military history and routinely “reenacts historical battles,” but said that Husted “quickly” opted to remove him from his staff after learning of the posts.

“While he denies negative intent, [Woytek’s] social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Sen. Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Sen. Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.”

Woytek also maintained public Spotify playlists with songs honoring the now-defunct nation of Rhodesia, which is revered by white supremacists online.

The former staffer expressed in a statement to The Post that he should have exercised better judgment on social media, and did not want to distract from Husted’s race.

“I want to be unequivocal,” Woytek told The Post before he was fired. “I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments.”

entries.title: Complaint Says Dozens of Congressional Candidates Failed to File Financial Disclosures
entries.summary: A new complaint by Campaign Legal Center knocked candidates for failing to file legally required reports detailing financial assets, liabilities and more.
entries.content:
More than 70 congressional candidates whose names will appear on the general election ballot in November failed to file legally required personal financial disclosures, according to new complaints filed with the House and Senate ethics committees on Friday.

According to the complaints, filed by the Campaign Legal Center, 66 House candidates and 11 Senate candidates missed the deadline to disclose assets, liabilities, book deals and other financial information that all candidates and lawmakers have to file.

Candidates are required to file these disclosures by May 15, or within 30 days of becoming a candidate, although they can request extensions up to 90 days.

“When candidates fail to file their financial disclosure reports accurately and on time, they deprive voters of crucial information about the financial interests of those who hope to represent them,” the Campaign Legal Center wrote in its complaint to the House Ethics Committee. “In order to make an informed decision at the ballot box, voters need to know about any potential conflicts of interest their Congressional candidates may have, and whether the claims made to voters align with their personal finances.”

The Washington Sun analyzed the Senate and House disclosure databases to confirm none of the candidates had filed their personal financial disclosures. Several candidates told The Sun they were unaware of the requirement.

Oklahoma Democratic nominee N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, who is running against Republican Rep. Kevin Hern, said her campaign had been unaware of the filing requirement before The Sun reached out for comment.

“It is a genuine administrative oversight from a first time candidate who has never held political office and is learning the complexities that come with running a federal campaign,” Thomas wrote in a statement. “Once this was brought to our attention, we immediately began reviewing the requirements and taking the necessary steps to correct the issue.”

Greg Howard Jr., the campaign co-chair for Amanda Pusczek, a Democratic congressional candidate in Alabama, told The Sun that the missed filing was “an unintentional administrative oversight on our end” and that the campaign was working to submit a disclosure.

The vast majority of the candidates who have failed to file are running in districts where their campaigns are considered long shots, as categorized by the Cook Political Report.

At least one candidate who has failed to file, Republican state Rep. Mark Tedford, the nominee in Oklahoma’s solid-red 1st Congressional District, is expected to win his seat in November.

The Tedford campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

But several other campaigns got back to The Sun, saying the missed disclosures were honest oversights.

The campaign spokesperson for Whitfield Harrington Jr., an independent candidate in Illinois, thanked The Sun for bringing the issue to their attention and said the team would be “contacting the appropriate officials to clarify the requirement, determine the applicable deadline, and make certain that any necessary action is handled promptly and through the proper process.”

Jeff Wadlin, a Libertarian Party Senate candidate in Arkansas, told The Sun that his accountant will file the financial disclosure in the coming days.

“As a third-party candidate, I didn’t know this was a requirement until recently,” Wadlin said.

Justin Murphy, the Republican nominee challenging incumbent Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), told The Sun that his campaign had “filed the required preliminary disclosure paperwork with the appropriate committee, and we are awaiting further instruction from them on filing the required financial disclosure.”

Kyle Austin, the Libertarian nominee in Montana’s Senate race who was cited in the complaint, questioned why the Senate hadn’t notified him when he missed the deadline.

“They haven't put any effort into it, so the question is, do they even really care?” Austin said.

The other six candidates cited in the complaint did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Sun.

“Failing to enforce violations of the House’s transparency requirements may incentivize others to ignore the law,” the Campaign Legal Center wrote in the complaint. “The Ethics Committee should also provide updated guidance making the filing requirements and the penalties for not filing timely and accurate disclosure reports clear.”

Tom Rust, chief counsel and staff director for the House Ethics Committee, declined to comment. The offices of Senate Ethics Committee chair James Lankford and vice chair Chris Coons did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
